q7.answer: Each instance polls the registry for the routing config every 10 seconds on a background thread and keeps an in-memory copy. If active or previous names a version it does not hold, it loads that artifact on the background thread while requests keep using the current model, then swaps the pointer atomically once the load succeeds. No redeploy is needed. The switch takes up to one poll interval plus load time.

q8.answer: The API puts the whole feature record it read in step 2 into the shadow message, together with the active output. The worker runs the candidate on that snapshot, so there is no second lookup and the candidate sees exactly what the active model saw. Shadow adds no latency because the message is queued only after the response is written. It goes into a bounded, non-blocking in-process buffer, and a background thread ships it to the queue. Inference runs in separate workers, and all errors are caught so none reach the response.

q9.answer: Backlog just waits in the queue, because workers scale and fail independently of the API. If the in-process buffer is full or the queue is unreachable, the API drops the message and increments a counter, and the user is unaffected. Drops shrink the sample and are reported as a drop rate, separate from candidate errors. A high drop rate raises an alert, and the on-call engineer may use the kill switch. There is no automatic disable. I did not set queue or buffer sizes, because the brief gives no request rate.

q10.answer: Shadow workers write one row per request to a results store, keyed by request ID. The row holds candidate_items, active_items, candidate_latency, errors or skip reason, feature_age and the shadow_salt of the run. Active predictions are carried in the shadow message and copied into that row, so both sit side by side. The hourly evaluation job counts only rows with the current run's salt. It computes error rate, p99 latency, days in shadow, skip rate and drop rate. It also computes overlap@20, rank correlation, share of empty or short lists and catalogue coverage against the active model. These show how different the candidate is, not whether it is better. The job writes a gate report to the registry.

q11.answer: There are four layers. (1) The registry lists each version's required feature names. (2) The materialization union is rebuilt from the routing config each run and includes the candidate as soon as it is set, even at percent 0. (3) The start of shadow has two phases, and the feature check runs in phase 2 and again at the promotion gate. The check samples records and blocks if any required feature appears in no sampled record. (4) The per-request check is the real guarantee. The worker checks that the snapshot has every required feature and is under 6 hours old, and otherwise records a skip and does not run the model. For the active model, step 2 returns a missing_feature fallback if the record lacks a required feature.

q12.answer: An on-call engineer runs the rollback command. It swaps the two routing config fields: active becomes the old previous, and previous becomes the old active. It needs no approval. Instances poll every 10 seconds, and both active and previous are always resident in memory, so the switch is only a pointer swap with no load. That is how it meets the 1-minute requirement, at about one poll interval plus swap time. Both versions stay in the materialization union, so their features remain available. Rolling back to anything older than previous needs a load and is not guaranteed to fit in 1 minute.
